Dual active sites with synergistic valence state regulation under oxidizing and
reducing conditions are essential for catalytic reactions with step-wise
mechanisms to modulate the complex adsorption sites of reactant molecules on
the surfaces of heterogeneous catalysts with maximized catalytic performances,
but it has been rarely explored. In this work, uniformly dispersed CuCo alloy and
CoO nanosheet composite catalysts with dual active sites are constructed, which
shows huge boost in activity for catalyzing water-gas shift reaction (WGSR), with
a record high reaction rate reaching 204.2 μmolCO gcat.
−1 s−1 at 300 °C for
Cu1Co9Ox amongst the reported Cu-based and Co-based catalysts. A synergistic
mechanism is proposed that Coδ+ species can be easily reduced by CO adsorbed
on Cu and Co0 can be oxidized by H2O. Systematic in situ characterization
results reveal that the addition of Cu can regulate the redox properties of Co
species and thus modulate the adsorption properties of catalysts. Particularly,
doping of Cu0 sites weakens the afﬁnity of the surface to CO or CO2 to a mod-
erate level. Moreover, it also promotes the oxidation of *CO to *COOH and the
desorption of the product CO2, reducing the carbon poisoning of the catalyst
and thus increasing the reactivity. The results would provide guidance for the
construction of novel heterogeneous catalyst with dual active sites and clarify its
underlying reactivity enhancement mechanism induced by the tunning of
valence state of metal centers for heterogeneous catalytic reactions.
Water-gas shift reaction (WGSR) is a signiﬁcant strategy for H2 pro-
duction and CO removal in ammonia synthesis or syngas conversion
reaction1–3. H2O serves as the oxidant for CO and the sluggish kinetics
make H2O dissociation be the rate-determining step4. Therefore,
constructing catalysts with favorable CO adsorption capacity and H2O
dissociation performance is a practical route to catalyze the WGSR at
low and medium temperature. Among them, transition metals are
encouraging due to the rich resource and low cost5. The reported Cu-
based catalysts for WGSR have mainly focused on supported catalysts,
which played a critical role in constructing interfacial sites and

improving stabilization by anchoring active metals on the surface of
oxide supports6–8. Zhang et al. reported that the strong metal support
interaction of Cu/CeO2 facilitated charge transfer to stabilize Cu+ for
CO adsorption due to the spontaneous Ce3+/Ce4+ change9. Jia et al.
found that the small CeO2 nanoparticles could formabundant CeO2-Cu
bulk-nano interfaces to facilitate the H2O dissociation and CO
oxidation10. However, catalysts composed of transition metal alloy and
corresponding mechanisms have rarely been reported for WGSR.
Exploring catalysts with dual active sites and tuned valence state is a
great challenge but also full of scientiﬁc and technological signiﬁcance.
Constructing dual active sites is also an efﬁcient strategy for
composite catalysts to serve as different roles in adsorption and con-
version of reactant molecules11–13. For WGSR, CoOx with active redox
properties is promising to collaborate with Cu due to the high activity
of O species for H2O dissociation14–16. Gu et al. reported that the special
coordination environment of octahedrally coordinated Coδ+ located in
a more open framework site made Co more accessible to oxygen and
possess active redox properties17. Jia et al. found that the surrounded
presence of small CeO2-x islets around Co could help construct CeO2-x/
CoO1-x interface and facilitate the H2O dissociation because the
defective structures Ov derived from spontaneous Ce3+/Ce4+ change
provided activated O species to modulate the oxidation state of Co
atoms18. Guo et al. revealed that Co could tune the d electronic
structure of Ni through the Jahn-Teller effect and thus the valence state
oscillated in monolayer NiCo hydroxides, which contributed to the
dynamic generation of active sites19. In other words, the heteroatom
doping could not only be the additional active sites for heterogenous
catalysis, but also modulate the electronic states of catalysts with
tuned valence state and dynamic active sites.
Herein, this work developed Cu/Co-CoO1-x composite oxides with
dual active sites for catalyzing WGSR, which greatly increased CO
conversion below 250 °C. The reaction rate of Cu1Co9Ox catalyst
reached 204.2 μmolCO gcat.
−1 s−1 at 300 °C, which was much higher than
the rate of the reported Cu-based and Co-based catalysts. Systematic
in situ characterization and DFT calculation results revealed that the
addition of Cu could tune the valence state of Co species and thus
modulate the adsorption properties of catalysts, which realized highly
efﬁcient catalytic performance for WGSR. The novel discoveries in this
work suggested a practical strategy to construct synergistic dual active
sites in heterogeneous catalysts and offered better understanding
about the mechanism of dual active sites thereof.
Results and discussion
Catalytic performance of CuaCobOx catalysts in WGSR
Series of CuaCobOx (a: b was the molar ratio of Cu to Co) catalysts were
synthesized via the hydrothermal method. The actual molar ratio of
Cu/Co was in scaling relation with the theoretical molar ratio, con-
ﬁrming the controllable synthesis strategy (Supplementary Fig. 1a).
Figure 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1b showed the catalytic activity of
catalysts with different ratios for WGSR with a high space velocity of
84,000 mL g−1 h−1. After the addition of Cu, Cu1Co9Ox exhibited much
higher activity than pure Co3O4 and catalysts composed of other ratios
without any production of by-product CH4 (Supplementary Fig. 2). The
CO conversion reached 100% at 250 °C for Cu1Co9Ox while that of pure
Co3O4 catalysts was around 12%, suggesting synergetic effect present
between Cu and Co-related species. Figure 1b compared the reaction
rate at 250 °C and 300 °C (Supplementary Table 1) and the reaction
rate of Cu1Co9Ox catalyst reached 204.2 μmolCO gcat.
−1 s−1 at 300 °C
which surpassed most reported catalysts of transition metals5,6,9,10,20–22.
The performance towards catalyzing WGSR for the Cu1Co9Ox and
Co3O4 catalysts was also evaluated under full reformate gas with feed

the kinetic catalytic process of WGSR. Furthermore, the CO and H2O
reaction order was measured in kinetic interval at 240 °C to investigate
the adsorption and conversion of reactants (Fig. 1e, f). The CO reaction
order of the Cu1Co9Ox catalyst (−0.07) was closed to 0, which indi-
cated that the CO conversion was barely inﬂuenced by the CO con-
centration because of the proper CO adsorption capacity and efﬁcient
conversion. In comparison, the CO reaction order of the pure Co3O4
catalyst was −0.73, indicating the severe CO poisoning, which was
consistent with the stability test. CO poisoning could be interpreted
that carbon-containing species like carbonates would be formed with
the adsorption of CO on the surface. To conﬁrm it, Ar-TPD was per-
formed after WGSR to investigate the decomposition of carbon-
containing species by monitoring MS signal of CO2 (m/e = 44). As
shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, the formation of CO2 could reﬂect the
decomposition of carbon-containing species. The higher coverage of
carbon-containing species on the Co3O4 surface could block the active
sites and then inhibit the WGSR. Besides, the texture structure of
Co3O4 maintained as nanosheet after WGSR, which could exclude the
inﬂuence of aggregation on the stability. Therefore, the enrichment of
poisoning species during reaction induced the reducing activity
towards catalyzing WGSR. The H2O reaction order of Cu1Co9Ox (0.30)
was smaller than that of the pure Co3O4 catalyst (0.58), indicating the
easier H2O adsorption and dissociation on Cu1Co9Ox catalyst4.
Structural evolution of the CuaCobOx catalysts
From the TEM images, it could be seen that the Cu1Co9Ox samples
showed irregular nanosheet stacking with sizes around 147.7 nm and with
thickness around 32.4 nm (Supplementary Fig. 6). In comparison, pure
Co3O4 obtained by the same method of synthesis were also present in
nanosheet morphology. It was found that a porous structure appeared
on the surface due to the high temperature dehydration of the sample
annealed in air. The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) analysis using N2
isotherms showed that the speciﬁc surface area of fresh Co3O4 and
Cu1Co9Ox catalysts was 83.2 and 61.8 m2 g−1, respectively (Supplementary
Fig. 7). The porous nanosheet structure with large speciﬁc surface area
provided more active sites for accelerating the diffusion and mass
transfer of reactants23,24. The light decrease of speciﬁc surface area for
fresh Cu1Co9Ox catalyst was attributed to the occupation of Cu within the
pores of Co3O4. The EDS-mapping results showed that the Cu and Co
elements obtained by this synthesis method dispersed uniformly and no
obvious aggregation was seen (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). Therefore,
the similar lattice parameter of CuCo made it easy to disperse two kinds
of elements evenly and facilitate the formation of interface between two
category metals. XRD results and the Raman results showed that Co3O4
was the main phase of fresh Co3O4 and Cu1Co9Ox. (Supplementary
Figs. 10 and 11). Besides, XANES and EXAFS results also conﬁrmed that
the Co species of two fresh samples were mainly the phase of Co3O4
(Supplementary Fig. 12). To investigate the structural change during
WGSR, the aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM and XRD measurements
of catalysts after WGSR were performed. As shown in Fig. 2a, the lattice
distances of 0.18 nm, 0.20 nm and 0.24 nm was the lattice fringe of CuCo
(200), CuCo (111) and CoO (111), respectively14,25, demonstrating abun-
dant interface structures during WGSR. The similar lattice parameter of
Cu and Co made it possible that Cu was incorporated into the lattice of
Co, showing the lattice distortion in Fig. 2b. The lattice distortion could
change the coordination environment of Co species and thus facilitate
the tunning of their valence states. As shown in Fig. 2c and Supple-
mentary Figs. 13 and 14, the reduction of Cu2+ to Cu0 and Co3+ to Co2+ or
Co0 destroyed the nanosheet structure while Cu still dispersed uniformly
with Co without obvious aggregation. However, Co3O4 was just reduced
to CoO during WGSR with unchanged nanosheet morphology and no

during WGSR of Cu1Co9Ox and Co3O4 samples indicated that the Cu
species could cause the structural collapse of Co-O species and facilitate
the charge transfer of Co species with tuned valence state.
In situ XRD under 5%H2/Ar atmosphere was performed to investi-
gate the phase evolution of the Cu1Co9Ox and Co3O4 samples (Fig. 3b,
c). It was observed that the phase transformed from Co3O4 to CoO at
250 °C and to metallic Co at 300 °C for the Co3O4 catalyst. In dramati-
cally contrast, CoO and metallic Co phase appeared even at 200 °C for
the Cu1Co9Ox sample. Besides, H2-TPR was also conducted to compare
the reduction process of Cuδ+ and Coδ+ species (Fig. 3d). The higher
reduction temperature of TPR than in situ XRD was attributed to the fast
10 °C/min programmed-temperature velocity of H2-TPR test. Similarly,
all Cuδ+ and Coδ+ species were reduced before 430 °C for the Cu1Co9Ox
catalyst, while only a minority of Coδ+ species were reduced before
400 °C and most of them transformed to metallic Co between 400 °C
and 500 °C. The lower temperature of Co reduction indicated that the
Cu species facilitated the structural collapse of Co-O species at low
temperature, which played a critical role in the tunning of valence state
between Co0 and Co2+ for CO consumption and H2O dissociation during
WGSR. Furthermore, after H2 reduction pretreatment at 300 °C for
30 min (Fig. 3e), only a little H2 was consumed for the Cu1Co9Ox catalyst,
indicating that most Co existed in the form of metallic Co. After WGSR
treatment and reaching a steady state, H2-TPR test was conducted again
to clarify the valence state of Co (Fig. 3f). Compared with H2 con-
sumption after H2 reduction pretreatment, more H2 consumption was
observed after WGSR treatment. This indicated that the Co was partially
oxidized by H2O, which was corresponding to the process of H2O dis-
sociation. Besides, from the results of CO-TPSR in Fig. 3g, the peak at
175 °C with the generation of H2 was attributed to the reaction of CO
with hydroxyl, which conﬁrmed the hydroxyl formation on the surface
from H2O dissociation4. The peak at higher temperature was ascribed to
the reduction of Coδ+ species. The schematic illustration of structure
evolution of Cu1Co9Ox catalysts during WGSR was shown in Fig. 3h.

peak was comprised of Co2+ and Co3+ species peaks (Fig. 4d). After H2

the region from 531.0 eV to 534.0 eV was corresponding to species

Raman results (Fig. 4f), the peaks from 400 to 600 cm−1 and that of
680 cm−1 also conﬁrmed the existence of Co-O species which played a
critical role to dissociate H2O30. The low peak intensity was attributed

From the above results, the dissociation of H2O could partially oxidize
the surface of the bulk metallic Co for Cu1Co9Ox catalyst with the
coexistence of Co0 and Coδ+ species on the surface to dissociate H2O
for catalyzing WGSR.
Reaction mechanism of Cu/Co-CoO1-x with dual active sites
To investigate the active sites and reaction mechanism, in situ DRIFTS
was performed. Under the reaction atmosphere of 2%CO/3%H2O/He, the
reaction temperature was gradually increased from 50 °C to 300 °C. As
shown in Fig. 5a–f, with the increase of temperature, the intensity of the
chemisorption peak of CO became stronger. For Co3O4, the CO
adsorption on Co was so weak that no adsorption signal was observed
and the peak of 2143 cm−1 was corresponding to baseline shift rather than
the CO adsorption on Co (Supplementary Fig. 19). In comparison, CO
adsorption was only observed on the Cu0 sites for Cu1Co9Ox without any
signals of Co0 or Co2+ sites, which was consistent with the results of CO
adsorption under 2%CO/He at 240 °C (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21).
Therefore, the in situ DRIFTS of CO adsorption suggested that the che-
misorption site of CO under the reaction conditions or pure CO atmo-
sphere was Cu. Figure 5c, f showed the carbon containing intermediates
from 1000 to 1800 cm−1 and the peaks were identiﬁed according to the
literature results (Supplementary Table 3). With the same ﬂow velocity
and peak intensity of CO, the intensity of carbon-containing inter-
mediates for Co3O4 was much stronger than that of Cu1Co9Ox catalyst
according to the scale bar of 0.03 and 0.002, respectively, indicating that
the surface of Co3O4 was blocked by carbon containing intermediates
easily. Besides, from the results of CO-TPD in Supplementary Fig. 22a–c,
carbon-containing intermediates formed from CO adsorption pretreat-
ment on the surface of Cu1Co9Ox catalyst could decompose into CO2 and
H2 at lower temperature than that of Co3O4 catalyst. This indicated that
Cu could facilitate the decomposition of intermediates like formate or
carboxylate species to minimize the carbon poisoning, which was con-
sistent with the stability test. The product CO2 of both catalysts could
also desorb from the surface at low temperature, avoiding the blockage

of active sites (Supplementary Fig. 22d). To conﬁrm it theoretically,
density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on CuCo
alloy, cobalt metal, and CoO (Supplementary Figs. 23–25). As displayed in
the Gibbs Free energy diagram (Fig. 5g), compared with pure Co or CoO,
the doping of Cu0 sites weakened the afﬁnity of the surface to CO or CO2
to a moderate level. Moreover, it also promoted the oxidation of *CO to
*COOH and the desorption of the product CO2, reducing the carbon
poisoning of the catalyst and thus increasing the reactivity. These con-
tributed to the reduction of the energy change in the most endothermic
step from 1.48 eV for CoO and 0.89 eV for Co to 0.44 eV for CuCo. In
conclusion, the doped Cu0 site was the active center of the Cu1Co9Ox
catalyst and promoted the decomposition of carbon species, in line with
the experimental observations.
It is common sense that catalysts follow redox mechanism or
associative mechanism for WGSR31–33. For the redox mechanism, CO
molecules preferred to react with surface oxygen with the production
of CO2 and oxygen vacancies which were the active sites for dis-
sociating H2O to form H2. For the associative mechanism, CO preferred
to react with adsorbed OH* on the surface from H2O dissociation to
form intermediate like formate or carboxylate species, whose
decomposition could produce CO2 and H2 simultaneously. The main
distinguishment of two mechanism is that the produced H2 could be
observed during the H2O dissociation process for the redox
mechanism10,34. Therefore, H2O surface reaction experiment was per-
formed (Supplementary Fig. 26). After in situ WGSR treatment to form
stable surface structure, no H2 was detected in the thermostatic test
under 3%H2O/He atmosphere 240 °C, excluding the potential redox
mechanism. To conﬁrm the associate mechanism, CO surface reaction
was performed. After being hydroxylated by H2O, CO could react with
surface OH* to generate CO2 and H2. As shown in Fig. 6a, CO ﬁrstly
reacted with lattice O to release abundant CO2 without H2. The high
reactivity of surface and lattice O could also be conﬁrmed by CO
DRIFTS where CO could quickly react with O which was accompanied
by the emergence of CO2 signal. The associate mechanism could be
inferred from the concentration ratio of produced CO2/H2 (~2) when
the reaction reached a stable state. It indicated that CO reacted with
OH* produced by H2O dissociation on the surface to generate CO2 and
H*, following 2 CO + 2 OH* →2CO2 + H2

In order to investigate the critical intermediates, transient analysis
was utilized to investigate whether the carbon-containing species
acted as active intermediates or as spectator species. After reaching a
steady state, the feed gas was switched from the 2%CO/3%H2O/He to
the CO-free 3%H2O/He mixed atmosphere at 240 °C. H2O would dis-
sociate and react with the carbon-containing species on the surface.
The conversion process of the carbon-containing intermediates was
monitored by in situ DRIFTS (Fig. 6b, c and Supplementary Fig. 27). The
spectra at 0 min were the results of the stabilization of the surface
species before the gas switching. Within the ﬁrst 2 min, the signals of
gaseous CO and adsorbed CO on the Cu sites disappeared rapidly. At
8 min, it could be found that only the intensity of formate and car-
boxylate species decreased with the generation of CO2, while the
intensity of allthe other carbonate species did not change signiﬁcantly.
This suggested that adsorbed CO would react with OH* to form for-
mate and carboxylate as the critical intermediates, which decomposed
to produce CO2 and H2, following the associate mechanism for WGSR.
Furthermore, to clarify the role and reaction of CO* and OH* on
the surface, cyclic CO-TPR experiments for observing the production
of CO2 and H2 for the Cu1Co9Ox catalyst were performed. (Between
CO-TPR-1 and CO-TPR-2, the catalyst was treated under 3%H2O/Ar
atmosphere at 300 °C for hydroxylation). As shown in Supplementary
Fig. 28, for the CO-TPR-1, the broad peak of CO2 was mainly con-
tributed to the reduction of CoOx and the production of H2 was
also observed due to the reaction of CO and OH on the surface. In
CO-TPR-1, the hydroxyl species formed during the synthesis process.
For the CO-TPR-2 after hydroxylation, accordingly, the co-production
of CO2 and H2 indicated that the generation of surface hydroxyl was
recyclable and WGSR followed the associate mechanism that CO
reacted with the hydroxyl. Therefore, the hydroxyl OH* and CO* on the
surface could react with each other to form formate and carboxylate
intermediates whose decomposition produced H2 and CO2. Wherein
the dissociation of H2O to form OH* was essential for the formation
and decomposition of formate and carboxylate intermediates.
The in situ DRIFTS results showed that Cu0 site of the Cu1Co9Ox
catalyst was the active center to adsorb the CO molecules under the 2%
CO/He and 2%CO/3%H2O/He reaction atmosphere without CO adsorp-
tion signal of Co sites. Furthermore, the transient analysis of in situ
DRIFTS, H2O surface reaction and CO surface reaction conﬁrmed the
associate mechanism for WGSR. Therefore, it was inferred that the
valence shift between Co0 and Coδ+ was the key factor for H2O dis-
sociation. The in situ Raman spectra was conducted to observe the
stepwise transformation of Co-O species by switching atmosphere
(Fig. 6e, f). The two fresh samples both exhibited the vibration mode of
Co3O4. The disappearance and reocurrence of Co-O vibration mode
between 400 and 600 cm−1 meant the complete reduction and partial

(Fig. 6d). Exposed with 2 mbar 10%CO/Ar, Coδ+ species were all reduced
to Co0 for the Cu1Co9Ox catalyst. After introducing 2 mbar 5%H2O/Ar,
Co0 was quickly oxidized to Coδ+ species where Co2+ was more stable for
the Cu1Co9Ox catalyst from the peak position. Subsequently, Co species
was completely reduced again under 2 mbar 10%CO/Ar of second cycle,
which was consistent with the in situ Raman spectra results. However,
from the quasi in situ XPS and linear combination ﬁt of XANES, the
coexistence of Co0 and Co2+ for Cu1Co9Ox under stable state conﬁrmed
that the valence state of Co species oscillated during WGSR, which was
corresponding to the sequential reduction and oxidation reactions
during WGSR. Therefore, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 6g, the
existence of Cu was conducive to the tunning of valence state between
Co0 and Coδ+ to facilitate the CO oxidation and the H2O dissociation.
In summary, this work constructed a uniformly dispersed Cu/Co-
CoO1-x composite oxides catalyst with dual active sites. Based on these
investigations mentioned above, Cu was the active site to adsorb CO
which reduced the surrounding Coδ+ species and H2O could thus oxi-
dized the surrounding Co0 species on the surface. In addition, Cu
enabled Co species with tuned valence state and proper valence states
under oxidizing and reducing conditions. Furthermore, Cu could sta-
bilize the surface of Co and was conducive to the decomposition of
carbon-containing intermediates, diminishing CO poisoning. The
favorable CO adsorption capacity of Cu and the tunning of valence
state between Co0 and Coδ+ could facilitate CO oxidation and H2O
dissociation, thus signiﬁcantly boosting the catalytic performance
towards WGSR. This work provides a unique approach to construct
and investigate chemical states oscillation between synergistic dual
active sites for governing surface kinetics and catalytic reactivities over
multi-component catalyst systems.
Methods
Synthesis of copper-cobalt catalysts
The copper-cobalt catalysts were prepared by the hydrothermal
method.
Firstly,
a
certain
amount
of
Cu(NO3)2·3H2O
and
Co(NO3)2·6H2O with the different ratios were dissolved in 39 mL dis-
tilled water and the pH value of the solution was controlled to ca.10 by
NaOH (4 mol L−1). After stirring for 15 min, the obtained suspension was
transferred to a Teﬂon-lined steel autoclave and kept at 100 °C for
24 h. The obtained precipitates were collected by centrifugation until
the pH was 7 and dried at 70 °C overnight. Finally, the CuaCobOx cat-
alysts were obtained by calcination at 300 °C for 2 h.
Catalytic performance evaluation towards WGSR
The catalytic performance towards WGSR was evaluated in a
continuous-ﬂow ﬁxed-bed reactor at 1 bar. A total of 50 mg of the
80–200 mesh catalysts mixed with 1 g of 40–70 mesh quartz sand was
ﬁrst placed in a quartz tube with an interior diameter of 1 cm. Then, a
thermocouple was inserted into the extra 1 g quartz sand layer to
obtain an accurate reaction temperature. Before the WGSR, the sam-
ples were reduced in 5%H2/N2 at 300 °C for 30 min, followed by
cooling to 100 °C naturally. Subsequently, a mixture of 2%CO, 10%H2O
and 88%N2 was fed into the reactor at 70 mL/min, together with tem-
perature programming from 150 to 300 °C. The CO conversion was
analyzed using an online GASBOARD gas analyzer. The CH4 generation
was analyzed by a gas chromatography.
The CO conversion was calculated according to the following
equation:
CO conversion = amount of CO converted ðmolÞ
amount of fed CO ðmolÞ
ð1Þ
The CH4 selectivity was calculated according to the following
equation:
CH4 selectivity = amount of CH4 produced ðmolÞ
amount of fed CO ðmolÞ
ð2Þ
The reaction rate (r) was calculated according to the following
equation:
rcatalyst =
amount of CO converted ðmolÞ
reaction time sð Þ × mass of catalyst ðgÞ
ð3Þ
Other kinetic studies were tested in the same reactor, and the CO
conversion was controlled below 15%. In detail, the activation energy
was calculated according to the reaction rates of different tempera-
tures in the kinetic range. The reaction order was calculated according
to the reaction rates of different feed gas compositions. As for the CO
reaction order, the H2O concentration was maintained at 20% and the
CO concentration was adjusted from 1.5 to 3% in 0.5% increments.
Similarly, as for the H2O reaction order, the CO concentration was
maintained at 3% and the H2O concentration was adjusted from 2.5 to
10% in 2.5% increments. The N2 ﬂow rate was adjusted simultaneously
to keep the total ﬂow rate of the feed gas at 70 mL/min.
X-ray diffraction (XRD)
The ex situ XRD patterns were acquired by the PANalytical X’pert3
powder diffractometer. The in situ XRD patterns were obtained from
the same machine with an Anton Paar XRK-900 reaction chamber. The
in situ reaction camber was heated from room temperature to 200,
250, 300 and 400 °C under 5%H2/Ar (30 mL min−1). Two rounds of tests
lasting for 20 min and 40 min were carried out for each selected
temperature. The 40 min measurement was obtained to investigate
the phase structure of the catalysts.
Temperature-programmed H2 reduction (H2-TPR)
H2-TPR with different pretreatments data were obtained by the
Quantachrome autosorb-iQ instrument. For normal H2-TPR, 50 mg of
the sample was ﬁrst purged with a He ﬂow at 150 °C for 1 h. For H2-TPR
after reduction at 300 °C, 50 mg of the sample was ﬁrst reduced with a
5% H2/Ar ﬂow at 300 °C for 30 min. For H2-TPR after in situ WGSR,
50 mg of the sample was ﬁrst reduced with a 5% H2/Ar ﬂow at 300 °C
for 30 min and then exposed with the 2%CO/3%H2O/Ar ﬂow at 300 °C
for 1 h. After different pretreatments, the catalysts were reduced with a
5% H2/Ar ﬂow from 50 to 600 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min. The signal was
collected using a thermal conductivity detector (TCD).
Temperature-programmed desorption (TPD)
TPD data were acquired using a Quantachrome autosorb-iQ instru-
ment. For CO-TPD, 300 mg of the catalysts was ﬁrst reduced by 5%H2/
Ar at 300 °C for 30 min and then purged with a He ﬂow, followed by
cooling to 50 °C. Then, the sample was adsorbed with CO under a 5%
CO/He ﬂow for 60 min. After removing the physical adsorption of CO
by He purging, desorption of the chemisorbed CO was achieved by
temperature programming from 50 to 800 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min.
The generation of H2 (m/z = 2), CO (m/z = 28) and CO2 (m/z = 44) were
detected by a mass spectrometer. For CO2-TPD, the test process was
same except that the adsorbed gas was substituted with CO2.
CO and H2O surface reaction
An online mass spectrometer (Ametek LC-D200M) was used to analyze
the outlet gases for surface reaction. 100 mg of sample was reduced
with 5% H2/Ar at 300 °C for 30 min and then went through WGSR for 1 h
at 300 °C. The catalysts were then purged by Ar at 240 °C, followed by
purging by 3%H2O/Ar for 1 h to observe H2O dissociation. After cooling
to 50 °C, 2%CO/Ar was purged under heating from 30 °C to 240 °C and

CO temperature-programmed surface reaction (CO-TPSR)
100 mg of sample was reduced with 5% H2/Ar at 300 °C for 30 min and
then went through WGSR for 1 h at 300 °C. The catalysts were then
purged by Ar and cooled down to room temperature. CO-TPSR was
performed by purging by 2%CO/Ar under heating from 30 °C
to 800 °C.
Raman test
The ex situ and in situ Raman spectra were tested by the LabRAM
HR800 spectrometer (HORLBA Jobin Yvon) using 473 nm laser exci-
tation. The in situ reactor (Xiamen TOPS) was used for in situ tests.
Before each measurement, ca. 25 mg of the catalysts were reduced in
5%H2/Ar at 300 °C for 30 min. For in situ Raman spectra under WGSR,
the catalysts were treated at 250 °C under 2%CO/3%H2O/Ar ﬂow. For
the switch test, the catalysts were exposed with 2%CO/Ar or 3%H2O/Ar
at 300 °C in turn.
X-ray absorption spectroscopy
Transmission XAS measurements were performed on a laboratory
device (easyXAFS300, easyXAFS LLC), which is based on Rowland
circle geometries with spherically bent crystal analyzers (SBCA) and a
silicon drift detector. Si (5,5,3) was used for Co K-edge measurement.
The powder samples were thoroughly ground and mixed with Boron
Nitride using an agate mortar and pestle and pressed into Ø = 10 mm
pellets. The pressed pellets were then sandwiched by Kapton tapes.
For the quasi in situ XAS, the catalysts were ﬁrstly reduced in 5%H2/N2
ﬂow at 300 °C for 30 min and then catalyzed WGSR at 300 °C for 1 h,
followed by cooling to room temperature. The treated samples were
transferred to a glovebox and prepared for XAS measurement without
direct exposure to air.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
The electronic structures of catalysts were investigated by using
an Axis Ultra XPS spectrometer from Kratos. For the quasi in situ
XPS, the catalysts were ﬁrstly reduced in 5%H2/N2 ﬂow at 300 °C
for 30 min and then catalyzed WGSR at 300 °C for 1 h, followed by
cooling to room temperature. The treated samples were trans-
ferred to a glovebox and prepared for XPS measurement without
direct exposure to air. The NAP-XPS (near-ambient pressure x-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy) measurement was performed on a
commercial SPECS NAP-XPS chamber equipped with a PHOIBOS
150NAP, 1D-DLD analyzer. The CuaCobOx catalysts were con-
ductive during NAP-XPS measurement, no charge was accumu-
lated on the surface of the catalysts. The catalysts were ﬁrst
reduced in 5%H2/Ar at 300 °C for 30 min. After cooling to the
room temperature, 2 mbar 10%CO/Ar and 2 mbar 5%H2O/Ar was
introduced, respectively.
In situ diffusion reﬂectance infrared Fourier transform spec-
troscopy (in situ DRIFTS)
In situ DRIFTS was carried out on a Bruker TENSOR 27 spectro-
meter between 1000 and 4000 cm−1. For any DRIFTS tests, cata-
lysts were ﬁrst reduced under 5%H2/He at 300 °C for 30 min and
then purged under He to remove any adsorbed species. For
temperature-dependent experiment, the temperature was chan-
ged in the sequence of 50 °C, 150 °C, 240 °C and 300 °C under 2%
CO/3%H2O/He. For transient analysis of intermediate species,
the feeding gas was switched from 2%CO/3%H2O/He to 3%H2O/He
at 240 °C for consuming adsorbed intermediate species. After 5%
H2/He reduction, CO adsorption experiment was performed
under 5%CO/He at 240 °C. The background spectrum was detec-
ted under a He ﬂow at reaction temperature and then subtracted
automatically in subsequent scans. 3%H2O is the saturated vapor
pressure of H2O at room temperature.
Computational details
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using
the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)35 based on the plane-
wave basis sets with the projector augmented-wave pseudo-potential
(PAW)36 method, with a 450 eV cutoff energy. The exchange-
correlation functional used was Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE)37
functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)38. For
metallic Co-Cu alloy, the Brillouin area was sampled by 3 × 3 × 1
Monkhorst–Pack mesh k-points, while for CoO it was 2 × 2 × 1, since
their surface energy converged slab model had different layers. In the
structure optimization, the force tolerance was set to 0.02 eV/Å, and
the convergence criteria of the total energy was set to 10−7 eV. In our
slab model, a large enough surface supercell (with only one absorbate)
was adopted such that the distance between the adsorbates was larger
than 10 Å, and a 15 Å vacuum layer was used to minimize the artiﬁcial
interaction between slabs on vertical direction. To simulate a dis-
ordered Cu-Co solid solution reduced from Cu1Co9Ox, we randomly
replaced 10% of the Co atoms by Cu atoms in the supercell. During the
structure optimization, atoms on the top layer in slabs were relaxed,
while the others were ﬁxed.
VESTA program was used in the pre- and post-processing of our
computations39. Vaspkit code was used to generate several calculation
ﬁles and calculate the correction of free energy40. The Gibbs free
energy
of
each
intermediate
was
estimated
according
to
G = E + EZPE + ΔU0→T – TS, where E is the electronic total energy at 0 K,
EZPE is the zero-point energy, ΔU0→T is the thermal energy correction at
ﬁnite temperature, and TS is the entropic contributions. The last three
terms result from the vibrational frequency calculations at 298.1 K,
where frequencies less than 50 cm−1 were set to 50 cm−1 to avoid
abnormal entropy contribution.
